html:
The Jadids were Muslim reformers in the Russian Empire, active from the 1880s to the 1920s, who wanted to modernise Muslim society through education. Their name comes from usul-i jadid, the "new method" of teaching children to read by sounds, not by rote.

The movement began with the Crimean Tatar Ismail Gasprinski, who opened a new method school in 1884 and published the newspaper Tercüman (The Interpreter). It spread to the Volga Tatars and, around 1900, to Turkestan and Bukhara. Jadids set up schools that taught geography, arithmetic and history along with religion, and started newspapers, theatres and publishing houses. They argued that Muslims had fallen behind through ignorance, not because of Islam. Conservative clergy and the Emir of Bukhara opposed them.

After 1917 many joined the Bolsheviks or ran short-lived governments, such as the Kokand Autonomy and the Bukharan People's Republic. Writers like Fitrat and Abdulla Qodiriy shaped modern Uzbek literature. The Soviets first used them, then killed most of them in the Great Purge of 1937 to 1938. Their ideas of nationhood fed into the Soviet republics drawn in 1924.
